reader.title: Killing of William Durant and lynching of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis
bases: After stockman William Durant was shot dead by a party of men, his armed friends hunted down and killed two neighbors suspected of leading that party, which the Evening Star headlined as a lynching (A1, A3, A4).

Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis were hunted down and killed by Durant's armed 'friends', with no officers or legal process mentioned, because they were suspected of leading the party that murdered Durant (A1, A3, A4). The group is plural but its size is never given, so the three-person threshold is not shown; Durant's own killing, by a party of men after a quarrel, carries no pretext of justice in the reports (A1).
Every report found is a copy or condensation of one Little Rock, Ark., dispatch of Nov. 19, with no local or independent account (A1, A3, A4, A9, A14).

summary.text: The killing of William Durant and lynching of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis took place near Tushomma, Indian Territory, in November 1888, when a stockman was shot dead outside his home and his friends then hunted down and killed two neighbors suspected of leading his killers.
Three men died, and no arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage.

A single wire dispatch from Little Rock, Arkansas, carried the story to papers from Washington to St. Paul, where headlines called the second killings a "lynching", "retaliation" or the work of "avengers".
William Durant was a stockman who lived near Tushomma in Indian Territory.
According to the dispatch, he had been quarrelling with two neighbors, Davis and Jeffries.
The reports give no cause for the quarrel and do not name the race of any of the men.
On Friday night, November 16, a party of men called Durant from his house and shot him in the yard, "riddling his body with bullets."
His friends, aroused by the killing, armed themselves and went after the two neighbors.
They "hunted down and killed" Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis, who were "suspected of having led the party that murdered Durant."
The dispatch, dated November 19, does not say when or how the two men were killed, how many took part, or whether any officer was involved.
No report of arrests, an inquest or any official response was found in the coverage, and no follow-up story was found.

The story ran almost word for word in white papers between November 19 and 28, first in the Washington Evening Star and the Alexandria Gazette and then in Richmond, Savannah, St. Paul, Camden and smaller towns.

Editors framed the same text in different ways: the Evening Star headlined "the lynching of two of his supposed assassins," while the Richmond Dispatch wrote "Swift Retaliation" and the Savannah Morning News "Two Men Suspected of a Murder Shot by Avengers."
The Camden Evening Telegram called it "An Indian Territory Vendetta," and the Middleburgh Post headed it "Two of the Assassins Killed," treating the suspicion against the dead men as settled.
The St. Paul Globe put the weight on the first killing, calling Durant's killers "Desperadoes" and Durant "an Innocent Stockman."

Shorter digests altered details as they condensed the dispatch: a Clarksville and a Maysville paper said the two men were hunted down "by the neighbors," and digests in Martinsburg and Connecticut moved the scene to Little Rock.
The full wire text names Durant's "friends" as the men who killed Jeffries and Davis, while two condensed paragraphs say "the neighbors"; the full text is the fuller and earlier version.
Most copies place the killing near Tushomma or "Tushoma," but the Camden paper printed "Tishomingo" and two digests mistook the Little Rock dateline for the scene.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Durant was murdered by a party of men after quarrelling with neighbors Davis and Jeffries; his friends armed themselves and killed the two men, who were suspected of having led the party.

accounts.label: Condensed 'Pointed Paragraphs' version
accounts.gist: Jeffries and Davis, suspected of having led the party, were hunted down 'by the neighbors' and killed.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined the 'lynching of two of his supposed assassins' over the unchanged wire text calling Durant's death a brutal murder.

Other headlines treated the killings as retribution: 'Swift Retaliation' (Richmond), 'Shot by Avengers' (Savannah), 'Two of the Assassins Killed' (Middleburgh), 'An Indian Territory Vendetta' (Camden).
The St. Paul Globe put the weight on Durant, calling his killers 'Desperadoes' and him 'an Innocent Stockman'.

conflicts.field: perpetrators of the killing of Jeffries and Davis
conflicts.note: The 'neighbors' wording appears only in a condensed paragraph of the same dispatch; the full wire text says friends and is the better evidence.
Little Rock is the dateline of the dispatch, misread as the scene by two digests; Tishomingo appears in one copy only.

record_check.dossier: William Durant, Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis; Jeffries and Davis are the victims of the lynching-type killing
lynching: no posse, officers or legal authority is mentioned; Durant's friends hunted down two suspects and killed them
probable lynching (killing of Jeffries and Davis on suspicion of Durant's murder; group size not stated)
Jeffries and Davis suspected of having led the party that murdered Durant
Durant's friends (for the killing of Jeffries and Davis); an unnamed party of men (for Durant)
revenge for Durant's assassination; the two were suspected of leading the party
Should add that Durant's friends then hunted down and killed Jeffries and Davis

info: Durant was killed on 'Friday night last' before the Nov. 19 dispatch, i.e. Friday, Nov. 16, 1888; the date of the killing of Jeffries and Davis is not given (between Nov. 16 and Nov. 19).
At Durant's home near Tushomma, Indian Territory (spelled Tushoma, Tusboms, Tusshoma; one copy says Tishomingo; two digests wrongly say Little Rock, Ark.)
William Durant, stockman, murdered by a party of men; Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis, neighbors, killed by Durant's friends
Jeffries and Davis were suspected of having led the party that murdered Durant; Durant had been quarrelling with them
Durant: an unnamed 'party of men'. Jeffries and Davis: Durant's 'friends' (two condensed versions say 'the neighbors')
